I hold that deploying it is right, provided the deciders assented only to what the evidence warranted; the opacity of the mechanism is not theirs to answer for. A judgement is sound when it assents only to what the impression warrants. If trials show the system reliably reduces suffering, assenting to that is sound, and it does not become unsound because the reasons inside the model cannot be written down for a patient.

The person decided about is not wronged by lacking an explanation, because their good never depended on it. What they owe themselves is a right response to what happens to them, and that response is fully in their power whether or not anyone explains the machine. Think of a triage tool that flags sepsis hours earlier than nurses do. The ward cannot say why it fires, but the trial data were checked carefully.

A Virtue Ethicist will object that justice is owed to the person a decision lands on, and a practice of withholding reasons trains deployers into people who stop thinking they owe anyone an answer. But the answer the deployers owe is an account of their own judgement, which they can always give: what evidence they saw and why they assented to it. That is owed and can be paid. An account of the weights inside the model was never theirs to give. If the deployment was judged with care on the evidence there was, the lack of an explanation takes nothing from its soundness.

Deploy it. The mechanism is an external, and the only thing anyone here is answerable for is how carefully they judged the evidence that it reduces suffering. What they owe themselves is a right response to what happens to them, and that response is fully in their power whether or not anyone explains the machine.

Epictetus divides the world into what is up to us and what is not. The inner workings of a trained model are not up to the people who deploy it. Their judgement about whether the evidence is good enough is up to them, and that is where their responsibility sits.

But the answer the deployers owe is an account of their own judgement, which they can always give: what evidence they saw and why they assented to it. That is owed and can be paid. An account of the weights inside the model was never theirs to give. An explanation would be welcome, yet nothing in the decision's soundness waits on it; only the weighing of the evidence does.

A Stoic can accept this motion. What matters is whether the people deploying it judged well, not whether the machine's workings can be laid out for everyone. Demanding an explanation before acting treats a feeling of understanding as if it were part of virtue. It is not. The deployers act well if they judged the evidence carefully and would withdraw the system the moment that evidence changed.

A clinic adopts a screening model after reading three independent audits. The model cannot explain a single case, but the clinic's judgement can be explained in full.

A Utilitarian will object that the Stoic has the right verdict for the wrong reason, since what justifies deployment is the suffering prevented and not the inner state of the people who chose it. Suffering prevented is a fine outcome, but outcomes are not up to anyone. A deployer who got lucky with poor evidence has not acted well, and one who judged soundly has, whatever the counts turn out to be. What was in the deployers' power was the judgement to deploy; whether the people decided about can follow its reasons was never part of that.
